en: In the tenth fascicle of the *Shi Dunlun Jizhuan Lunben*,

within the section on "Distinctions," the explanation of the seventh member, "Citing Causes" (*hetūpanibandha*), is concluded. From here below, the five members of "the producer and the produced" (*janaka-janyatva*) are explained.
The limb of craving (*tṛṣṇā-aṅga*) consists solely of greed (*rāga*) among the afflictions.
Although this [craving] takes both internal and external fruits as its objects, it is pervasive.
Most treatises take craving for external objects as their primary focus,
because it arises from the experience of objects and is produced by the delusion regarding the dominant fruit that results from being confused about those external objects.
The limb of grasping (*upādāna*) generally takes all afflictions as its intrinsic nature.
The nature of the four types of grasping has already been explained previously.
This limb consists exclusively of those afflictions that act as the grasper and the grasped within the process of grasping; it accords with the afflictions and does not include other phenomena.
The fifty-ninth [fascicle] states:
One should say that all afflictions within the entire realm are capable of linking rebirth and continuity.
Since craving (*tṛṣṇā*) is exclusively attachment (*rāga*), [how can it alone perform this function?]
Therefore, "grasping" (upādāna) is taken here as a comprehensive category that exhaustively includes all afflictions.
However, the explanation given here— that craving directed toward the four types of grasping constitutes the limb of grasping—
is identical to that in the *Daśabhūmika Sūtra*.
He said: "The intensification of craving is called 'clinging' (*upādāna*).
This is stated in the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi*.
In the stage of moistening karma, the power of craving (tṛṣṇā) increases preeminently;
craving is said to be like water because it is able to provide moisture.
Only through repeated irrigation can the sprout of existence (bhava-aṅkura) arise.
Furthermore, based on their initial and final stages, craving (*tṛṣṇā*) and grasping (*upādāna*) are distinguished as two separate factors.
Although the factor of grasping subsumes all afflictions (*kleśa*), craving is predominant in its capacity to moisten [the seeds of existence];
therefore, it is said that craving increases [in this stage].
The respective texts do not contradict one another.
This is because the two links of craving (*tṛṣṇā*) and grasping (*upādāna*)— both in their manifest and latent states— are equally capable of moistening [the seeds of existence],
and because craving serves as the causal condition (*hetu-pratyaya*) for grasping.
As for "perverse aspirations," those who seek rebirth in the higher realms as their nirvana while observing the prohibitive precepts—
this is called a perverse aspiration.
To give rise to craving toward precepts is called the clinging to rules and observances (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*).
This passage specifically identifies craving as one of the four types of clinging.
Question: What kind of rules and observances exist in the two upper realms that could give rise to craving?
The commentary states:
Non-Buddhists likewise adhere to precepts regarding body and speech within the realm of form;
in the formless realm, they also falsely establish precepts based on mental volition and adhere to them as such.
Among the links of dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*),
"existence at a prior time" refers to the interval between the moment of birth and the moment of death.
Since this text explains the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) separately from the five destinies (*gati*),
it is clear that the intermediate state is not subsumed within those destinies;
this is the same as the view of the Sarvāstivādins.
Although ten types of existence are enumerated,
the primary intent clarifies that "existence" refers specifically to existence within the desire realm.
The "limb" refers to the limb of formations (*saṃskāra*).
Because craving (*tṛṣṇā*) and grasping (*upādāna*) moisten it, it is capable of producing a future fruit; this is called "karmic existence" (*karma-bhava*).
This very capacity [to produce] is what is termed "existence" (*bhava*).
All others are present. According to the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi*,

from the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) until one reaches the fundamental existence (*mūlabhava*) before it undergoes decay and transformation, all are subsumed under the "birth" link (*jāti-aṅga*).
Thus, one should know that the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) is also included within the category of "existence" (*bhava*).
Regarding whether the intermediate existence and the birth-existence (*upapattibhava*) are produced by a single karma or by separate karmas,
I have not seen any textual evidence for Master Jing’s interpretation.
The text merely states that there is transformation within the intermediate state (*antarābhava*).
Based on this, one should know that the intermediate state is produced by a distinct karma;
yet, although this is said, it can also be described as being projected by a single karma.
The realm of form (*rūpadhātu*) consists of six existences, as it excludes the four destinies (*gati*);
the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*) consists of five existences, further excluding intermediate existence (*antarābhava*).
Now, this "existence" member (*bhavāṅga*) refers exclusively to the member of karma (*karmāṅga*).
It is said that because they are grasped by the afflictions (*kleśa*) through prior formative actions (*pūrva-kṛta-saṃskāra*), the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* states:

"The seeds of projecting karma and the causes of what is projected, when moistened by the conjunction of craving (*tṛṣṇā*) and grasping (*upādāna*), undergo transformation; this is termed 'existence' (*bhava*)."
Because both are capable of bringing about the fruit of future existence.
His intention is to say that the five factors—

volitional formations (*saṃskāra*), consciousness (*vijñāna*), and so forth— when they proceed through the moistening of craving (*tṛṣṇā*) and grasping (*upādāna*), are called the "existence" (*bhava*) link.
Its essence consists solely of seeds, for they are that which is moistened and that which is capable of producing fruit.
Now, this general statement "the ten possess existence" (daśa-sad-bhāva) means that the capacity to exist and that which exists are combined and termed "existence."
The general interpretation holds that there is meaning beyond merely interpreting the existence-branches (*bhavāṅga*);
here, it is specifically karma that constitutes one of these existence-branches.
The *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* explains this as follows:
In some places, it is taught that only the seeds of karma are called "existence" (bhava),
because they are what directly bring about the ripened fruit (vipākaphala).
He further reconciles this by stating:
Furthermore, there are those who maintain that only five types of existence (*bhava*) are called "existence" (*sat*),
because they serve as the seeds for the arising of future consciousness and so forth.
As for the seven existences, they consist of the five destinies (*gati*) as actual existences, because they involve the experience of the results [of karma].

Regarding the two intermediate states within the process of transition (*gati-upāya*), there are six because they constitute the "belonging-to" (the objects) and the "possessing-the-ability" (the subject);
since they are capable of projecting the various realms of existence (*bhava*),
these together constitute seven.
In the past, there was existence at death and existence at birth;
these are specifically designated as the existences of the five destinies (gati),
and therefore [existence at death] is not established separately.
Within the section on the factors of arising (*jāti-aṅga*),
first there is a detailed explanation of ten phrases,
followed by a summary of their meaning.
The first four lines describe the two modes of birth, namely womb-birth and egg-birth;
the subsequent line describes moisture-birth and transformation-birth.
These collectively refer to a single body as the "birth-link" (*jāti-aṅga*).
Regarding the phrase "the body parts arise all at once":
this treatise, as well as previous volumes and other sūtras and śāstras,
all state that those born by transformation arise instantaneously.
In the other three modes of birth, the sense faculties manifest gradually.
Now, since it is stated that moisture-born beings also arise instantaneously,
one should understand that for those born from wombs or eggs, the sense faculties arise gradually.
Beings born by transformation arise instantaneously.
Those born from moisture may arise either gradually or instantaneously.
As for the instantaneous type, it is like the emergence of moisture-born insects from decaying dampness that have not yet changed form, wherein their sense organs are all complete at once.
The final five phrases pertain to the existence of the four modes of birth (*catur-yoni*).
"Obtaining the aggregates" (*skandha-prāpti*) refers to the arising of the substance of the aggregates.
"Obtaining the elements" (*dhātu-prāpti*) refers to the seeds of the aggregates and their nature as causes and conditions for the aggregates.
The aggregates (skandhas) attain the maturation of manifestation;
the elements (dhātus) attain the maturation of seeds;
and the bases (āyatanas) attain both manifestation and seeds.
The remaining three conditions bring about maturation.
Within the summary of the meaning, there are six phrases:
two phrases concerning the essential nature, which comprise both production and manifestation.
The three phrases concerning birth, location, state, inclusion, and so forth, refer to the arising of the destinies (*gati*).
The single phrase concerning the inclusion of the aggregates (*skandha*) obtained by what is born refers to the aggregates themselves.
The two phrases concerning the inclusion of the elements (*dhātu*) and the inclusion of the bases (*āyatana*) obtained through causes and conditions refer to the causal conditions.
One phrase concerning the arising of the aggregates as they are sustained and subsumed;
one phrase concerning the manifestation of the life-faculty as it is supported by co-arising;
and two phrases for the members of old age and death.
First, aging is explained, followed by death.
Within the section on aging, seventeen phrases are first analyzed individually,
after which their summarized meaning is concluded.
There are ten phrases in the *saṃyojana* [section].
The first six phrases each subsume one phrase.
The seventh, "the deterioration of deportment" (*īryāpathavipariṇāma*), subsumes the subsequent five phrases.
The eighth [category], the immaterial faculties, is subsumed under the two phrases of the tenth and eleventh [sections].
The ninth, the material faculties, is subsumed under the fourteenth and fifteenth phrases.
The tenth period having passed and the lifespan being about to end is subsumed by the sixteenth and seventeenth verses.
Within the section on death, there is first a detailed explanation of eleven phrases,
followed by four phrases that conclude the summarized meaning.
If death is subsumed under the first two lines,
it is because they constitute the essential nature of actual dying;
if the dharma of death is subsumed under the third and fourth lines, [it is because they refer to the process leading up to it].
Regarding the factors of resolution and non-resolution:
because these are the rules for the manner of death in the five destinies,
the distinctions of death are subsumed under the sixth sentence following the fifth sentence.
Regarding the eleventh point, which is subsumed under the stage subsequent to death—
the "activity of the Lord of Death" (mṛtyu-māra)—
the Master Vasubandhu provides the following explanation.
This refers precisely to the essence of the process of dying, which is the activity of the Mara of Death.
This is also subsumed under the specific categories of death;
alternatively, it is because one takes the state after death—once consciousness has departed from the body—to be the "Mara of Death."
It is also said that these are subsumed under the state after death.
These two members, birth and death, have the five aggregates as their nature, as appropriate,
because they constitute manifest suffering.
The *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* states that this refers exclusively to active manifestations (*samudācāra*), though some interpretations include seeds as well;

furthermore, it maintains that from the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) until one reaches the fundamental existence (*mūlabhava*) and before any degeneration occurs, all stages are subsumed under the "birth" member (*jāti-aṅga*).
Among these, even if a transformative mind (*nirmāṇacitta*) arises at the final stage and takes the future fruit as its object, it is still the "birth" (*jāti*) link;

for, due to the craving and grasping (*tṛṣṇā-upādāna*) that preceded death, it has the capacity to moisten existence (*bhava*), thereby giving rise to the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) and the subsequent birth.
The various states of decay and transformation are collectively termed "aging.
The disintegration of the body and the end of life are termed "death.
Regarding the fifth [topic], the sequence of existence has three further repetitions.
Regarding the first "further explanation" (*punaḥ krama*),
concerning the statement that "due to misconduct,

the mind becomes inverted," one interpretation holds that the five members beginning with consciousness (*vijñāna*) are all explained in terms of the five present-arising members of cause (*hetu-aṅga*) within the subsequent limit (*aparānta*), specifically at the stage when birth, aging, and death are about to arise.
This is because it is not based on the five members as they exist in the causal stage.
The *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* states:
"Because the distinct characteristics [of the members] are difficult to discern during the causal stage, the five members are established separately by relying on their future resultant stage."
If one relies on this meaning,
"inversion of mind" refers to the fact that,
following the consciousness of karma, once it has arisen from form, it acquires the category of the commonality of sentient beings (nikāya-sabhāga).
Because that [consciousness] is what first receives birth as name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*).
As the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* states:
"The karmic seeds within consciousness are called the link of consciousness (*vijñāna-anga*)."
Therefore, the Tripiṭaka Master says:
"The final mind of the intermediate state (antarābhava) is called 'inverted' (viparyāsa),
because it can induce the invertedness of the projecting factors (ākṣepaka-aṅga)."
Within the fundamental consciousness (*mūlavijñāna*), the seeds of the link of consciousness (*vijñānāṅga*) are also termed the "inversion of mind" (*cittaviparyāsa*).
Because of this inversion of mind, the factors such as the linking of rebirth (*pratisaṃdhi*) are called "name-and-form" (*nāmarūpa*).
The perfection of the sense faculties refers to the link of the six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatanāṅga*).
The second is the enjoyment of the object, which refers to the members of contact (*sparśa*) and feeling (*vedanā*).
Because contact induces the arising of feeling, and both together enjoy the object,
the *Abhidharmakośa* calls this "feeling that follows contact" (*sparśānuparivartinī vedanā*).
Jing further explained:
"The six sense bases (ṣaḍāyatana) are the condition for contact (sparśa).

At the moment contact arises, it depends upon both the faculty (indriya) and consciousness (vijñāna), as well as the utilization of the object; thus, contact is produced from the conjunction of these three."
Therefore, it is said that there are two objects of enjoyment:
"attachment" refers to craving for the present,
while "seeking" refers to craving for the future.
These are collectively termed the link of craving (*tṛṣṇā*).
The flourishing of afflictions is called the link of grasping (*upādāna*).
In this context, karma alone is designated as the link of existence (*bhava*).
As previously established,
the remainder of the text is easily understood.
According to one interpretation, the sequence should be determined by combining the three time periods.
Ignorance, volitional formations, and consciousness belong to the past life.

Regarding those whose minds are inverted, the five factors beginning with consciousness are collectively termed "mind," because they are not separate from consciousness and because consciousness is predominant.
Because the mind is perfumed by misconduct and thereby gives rise to rebirth in the future realms of existence, it is called "perverted.
For brevity, the perfuming by correct conduct is not mentioned;

however, based on the subsequent fact that craving and grasping moisten the karma for future existence (*punarbhava*), one should know that they likewise moisten the mind of formations (*saṃskāra*) in the prior limit [of time].
Therefore, they are not discussed here in detail.

Regarding the past limit (*pūrvānta*), craving (*tṛṣṇā*), grasping (*upādāna*), and existence (*bhava*) are equivalent to name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*). The subsequent four links give rise to birth (*jāti*); these constitute the branches of birth and old age and death (*jarāmaraṇa*) in the past life.
The *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* states: "However, as for the results produced, if they pertain to the future, 'birth,' 'aging,' and 'death' are mentioned in order to induce revulsion.
If they pertain to the present, the five factors beginning with 'consciousness' are mentioned in order to bring about an understanding of how the stages of existence arise sequentially."
That [other system] states that the link of consciousness (*vijñāna*) first enters the mother’s womb;
this [system], however, speaks of name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*), and thus consists of only four links.
Through present craving (*tṛṣṇā*), the affliction of passionate attachment arises, which nourishes and moistens the karma for future existence (*punarbhava*).
Up to and including future existence, there will be birth, old age, and death.
However, only the moistening of karma is mentioned, not its origination;
this is because the origination of karma is understood by analogy with the past limit (*pūrvānta*).
This is to illustrate by way of analogy that in the past, one speaks of the initiation of karma but not its moistening;
in the present, one speaks of the moistening of karma but not its initiation;
and in the future, one speaks of birth, old age, and death but not of name-and-form and so forth.
In the present [teaching], name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*) and so forth are mentioned, while birth and old age/death (*jātimaraṇa*) are not;
this is stated because it seeks to demonstrate that the three time-periods of cause and effect are uninterrupted, and thus accords well with the Hīnayāna.
In the second instance, however, the establishment is based solely upon two time-periods.
The internal body as a condition is the gateway for the initiation of karma and the projection of rebirth;
the objective field as a condition is the gateway for the moistening of birth and the arising of its fruit.
That which gives rise to delusions such as the grasping at a self is the ignorance associated [with the mind].
"Or, arising from this, that is 'unshared delusion' (asādhāraṇa-moha).
Once the karma has been initiated, one immediately gives rise to many discursive thoughts (vitarka) and so forth in accordance with that karma.
Jing says: "Consciousness (vijñāna) is able to discern and differentiate; this is called discursive thought (vitarka)."
This is called the investigation into the arising of the seeds of name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*),
the six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*), contact (*sparśa*), and sensation (*vedanā*) from the branch of formations (*saṃskāra*);
for by means of that branch of formations assisting the seed of consciousness, it is able to successively induce these seeds.
This causes one to experience, in the future, similar fruits of suffering such as name-and-form (nāmarūpa) and so forth.

The *Bieyi* states: "Since bodily and vocal karma are initiated and mental karma arises through discursive thought (*vitarka*), they act as auxiliaries to the members of existence (*bhava*) and consciousness (*vijñāna*)."
The link of consciousness arises.
From this point onward, the three fruits gradually emerge.
Master Ji says that "those who frequently give rise to discursive thought (vitarka) in accordance with that karma" refers to the active consciousness (*pravṛtti-vijñāna*).
Because the seeds of consciousness are assisted by karma,
and because the seeds of name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*) and so forth are assisted by the seeds perfumed by karma— all of these are termed "consciousness."
These are capable of inducing the three types of suffering in the future:
first, the suffering of the initial arising of the faculties, which refers to the name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*) because each individual faculty—whether of body or mind—first arises;
second, the suffering of the perfection of the faculties, which refers to the six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*).
The third is the suffering of experiencing objects, which refers to contact (*sparśa*).
This is because it possesses two types of generative capacities through its association with names and phrases.
In reality, there should be two results: consciousness (*vijñāna*) and feeling (*vedanā*).
Because the seed of consciousness serves as the causal seed, it does not exist within the fruit.
As for sensation (*vedanā*), it is designated as "external" or "internal," yet it does not exist within the fruit;

this is because craving (*tṛṣṇā*) necessarily arises only by depending upon sensation, and thus sensation is absent at the prior limit (*pūrvakoṭi*) but said to exist at the subsequent limit (*aparānta*).
Because it is taught that one will experience [feeling] in the future based on contact in the past,
each has its own distinct basis.
Regarding the arising of craving conditioned by contact, this refers to the limb of craving (*tṛṣṇā-aṅga*).
The branch of grasping (*upādāna*) consists of the extensive pursuit and so forth arising from the enjoyment of objects.
By way of the door of activity,
this refers to those such as kings who perform rites of purification (*śauca-karman*).
Regarding the gateway of gain and offerings (*lābha-satkāra*):
this refers to sitting idly to collect [wealth], sowing seeds, plowing fields, and so forth.
These two, which arise from external objects of desire, are termed "seeking through desire" (*kāma-paryeṣaṇā*).
Alternatively, that which arises through the gateway of rules and observances refers to the grasping at rules and observances based on wrong aspirations; from this,
one gives rise to seeking within one's own body.
This is because one seeks the body as the fruit of future happiness;
or, it arises from the gate of liberation, meaning from the grasping at views (*dṛṣṭiparāmarśa*), by which one seeks false liberation.
One interpretation holds that the door of purposeful activity refers to the grasping for sensual desires;
the door of gain and honor refers to the grasping for views, as one clings to views as superior for the sake of gain and honor;
and the door of precepts and observances refers to the grasping for precepts and observances.
The gate of liberation refers to the grasping at a self-identity (*ātma-vāda-upādāna*).
Because one dwells in the truths and clings to the intrinsic nature of a self as being liberation,
these four types of grasping give rise to the three kinds of seeking.
1. Seeking much, because of seeking the five sensual desires;
2. Seeking within one's own body, which is seeking existence, because of seeking a self-identity;
3. Seeking false liberation, which is seeking a false holy life, because of seeking a false liberation.
Regarding the phrase "when seeking in this way, it causes the previously arisen afflictions, karma, and so forth":
this means that karma constitutes the *bhava-aṅga* (existence link),
and ignorance serves as the condition for initiating karma, causing future results to arise.
Ignorance is not a limb of existence (*bhavāṅga*).
Regarding the third section,
"by means of the three groups of sentient beings":
The previous two sections explained the sequence of saṃsāra alone;
now, this section speaks of the three aggregates based on both saṃsāra and its cessation.
Regarding those who delight in worldly purity:
Because one does not delight in the supramundane but delights in the realms of humans and devas, it is called "pure.
Nevertheless, due to ignorance, one may also perform non-meritorious actions;
or, the mental continuum may abide in a state induced by subsequent regret, or induced by joy that is free from regret.
Master Jing’s commentary states:
This refers to the presence or absence of remorse within the intermediate state (*antarābhava*).
It is the continuity of consciousness that abides and arises from formative volitions (*saṃskāra*) as consciousness.
Master Ji’s commentary states:
"As for 'regret,' it is because one delights in purity that one regrets non-meritorious actions."
Or, for one who is deluded and does not understand or repent,
the mental continuum— drawn forth by joy due to these three types of action—
abides as a continuum perfumed by the seeds of a joyful state of mind.
This refers to the link of consciousness (vijñāna) having this as its cause:
for those lacking merit, it is inferior karma;
for those possessing merit, it is middling karma.
Due to the superior karma of those who are immovable,
even in their future place of birth, they are able to bring about the fruits of all three types of suffering.
That which is termed the "seed" is the link of consciousness (*vijñāna*), while that which is termed the "manifestation" is name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*) and so forth.
The meanings of feeling (*vedanā*) and so forth are not explained here, as they follow the previous exposition.
"Attachment to sense objects" refers to feeling (*vedanā*), craving (*tṛṣṇā*), and grasping (*upādāna*).
That which has birth, aging, and death is called "existence" (bhava) due to its attachment to objects;
this is explained in full sequence in the *Pratītyasamutpāda-sūtra*,
but I shall not describe it here for fear of prolixity.
In the sixth section, "Explanation of Objections," there are two questions and answers.
Regarding the first question concerning the reverse order,
the response beginning with "Because it is based on this that the principle of the truths is proclaimed," and so forth, is as follows:
Contemplating old age, death, and so forth constitutes thirty-four types of knowledge (*jñāna*).
Among the Four Noble Truths, since old age and death are the first to be identified as suffering (*duḥkha*), one contemplates old age and death first.

The seeds of the five present factors, such as consciousness (*vijñāna*) and so forth, which have existed since beginningless time, are termed "ancient consciousness" and "ancient name-and-form" (*nāmarūpa*).
From this seed, that future birth as well as aging and death arise.
Within these two fruits, consciousness, name-and-form, and so forth are collectively termed "new" consciousness, name-and-form, and so forth.
Thus far, the linking of rebirth (*pratisaṃdhi*) through name-and-form has been explained in general.
The substance of name-and-form (nāmarūpa) is broad and subsumes the remaining members [of dependent origination];
thus, by mentioning "name-and-form" alone, the others have already been explained.
Regarding "liberation through the mind":
Because the formations (saṃskāra) branch of ignorance does not arise in the present life as a projecting cause,
the seeds of the [subsequent] five branches also do not arise in succession;
this is because the causes in the present do not arise in succession.
In the stage of old age and death, the five fruits—consciousness and the others—all perish in succession.
One should say that the new consciousness perishing is the primary factor, up to and including the perishing of sensation as the final factor.
However, because name-and-form (nāmarūpa) is taken as the preceding condition, it is referred to here as "new."
With the cessation of name-and-form as the primary factor, up to the cessation of feeling as the final factor;
furthermore, among the forty-four types of knowledge, one first contemplates old age and death through the contemplation of the Four Truths,
observing that birth is the origin of old age and death, which is the ancient name-and-form.
Because it arises prior [to birth], old age and death begin with birth; this is what is called "new name-and-form.
Now, observing that the cessation of the essence of old age and death is precisely the cessation of new name-and-form.
Among the twelve links, one first contemplates the cessation of old age and death as the primary focus.
The *Pratītyasamutpāda-sūtra* states:
"It is like a disease, its cause, the cessation of the disease, and the excellent medicine."
Therefore, the sequence is reversed, beginning with birth and old age and death.
To the question, "Why is it not stated that the cessation of ignorance is the primary [condition]?"—
this question refers to the preceding scriptural citation which states that the cessation of name-and-form is the primary [condition].
"Why does that sutra not state that ignorance is the first to be extinguished?
The answer, "Because it is established in dependence upon those whose minds are liberated," and so forth,
explains this meaning as follows:
Prior to entering the state of a noble one (*ārya*), during the initial stage of the equipment (*sambhāra-avasthā*), one first contemplates according to the forward order (*anuloma*).
Within the path of preparation (*prayoga-mārga*), one contemplates according to the reverse order (*pratiloma*), giving rise to forty-four cognitions (*jñāna*) and so forth.

Because one abandons [the afflictions] according to the forward order upon entering the path of seeing (*darśana-mārga*) and so on, it is said that "with the cessation of ignorance (*avidyā*), volitional formations (*saṃskāra*) cease," and so forth.
Based on the present name-and-form and sensation within the body of liberation of one beyond training (*aśaikṣa*),
the seeds of the four branches cannot act as causes to produce the fruits of birth, aging, and death in a future life.
This explains that the cause of suffering cannot arise.
The following clarifies that through the cessation of craving (*tṛṣṇā*), future suffering will not arise.

That is to say, when one who is liberated experiences objects in the present, craving and its latent tendencies—that is, the factors of craving and grasping (*tṛṣṇā-upādāna*)—are forever uprooted by the power of the Noble Path and do not arise again.
The name "the permanent cessation of the origin of afflictions (*kleśa-samudaya-satya*) which is capable of moistening" refers to the fact that because this cause is permanently ceased,
the seeds of name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*) and so forth, previously projected by causes, shall not produce further fruits;
this is termed "the cessation of the remaining members."
The meaning of this statement is to show that the seeds of present name-and-form do not produce future fruits,
because one first contemplates the Truth of Suffering;
thus, the cessation of name-and-form is made the primary focus.
By what is this cessation brought about?
It is by the cessation of that craving, grasping, and so forth— which are subsumed under the truth of origination and are capable of moistening [the seeds]—
that the seeds of name-and-form and so on will not produce their fruits.
Name-and-form and the other factors are the causes and conditions for birth, aging, and death in future lives.
Because they are the direct causes and conditions, these are said to cease first;
ignorance and the other remote factors are examined only later.
Because it is the moisture-conditioning cause (*ārdra-hetu*),
ignorance is not said to be the primary factor to be extinguished; therefore,
having attained the state of one beyond training (*aśaikṣa*), one observes as follows:
"By the absence of what is there the absence of old age and death?
and so forth; the subsequent sequence of cessations should be understood accordingly.
As for the statement, "one should understand that such categories explain the sequence of dependent origination," it means as follows:
Jingyun calculates that this concluding statement should have been made prior to the formulation of the objection;
however, because this objection was established within the section on the "Order of Sequence" (kramamukha),
the conclusion regarding the sequence of dependent origination is stated here after the objection.
In the seventh section, the explanation of terms, there are five successive expositions.
Regarding the explanation of the name based on its syllables:
it is called "dependent origination" (*pratītyasamutpāda*) because, conditioned by the fetters of the afflictions (*kleśa*), one repeatedly arises within the various realms of existence (*gati*).
Because it explains the term "dependent origination" (*pratītyasamutpāda*) by relying on the word "condition" (*pratyaya*), it is called "relying on the word.
Master Jing’s supplement states:
"That which, bound by various afflictions (*kleśa*), proceeds through the various realms of existence (*gati*)"—this explains the word "condition."
"Arising repeatedly" explains the term "arising.
As for the explanation based on the meaning of *kṣaṇa* (moment),
it serves to distinguish [this] from the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) dependent origination asserted by the Mahāsāṃghika, Mahīśāsaka, and other schools.
This also refutes the Saṃmitīya doctrine of the four characteristics occurring within a single period.

Regarding the phrase "the various conditions having passed away yet not being separated," if one relies on the ten prior members as conditions for the arising of the two subsequent members according to their sequential stages:
Although the four factors of the preceding limb, such as the causal conditions,
perish momentarily and enter the past,
because their seeds remain within the body and are not abandoned, they give rise to subsequent effects based upon that very body.
Alternatively, each of the twelve links may serve as a condition for, and arise from,
each of the others. The principle that "because this exists,
that exists" reveals the meaning of dependent origination without a creator.
The phrase "because this arises,
that arises" clarifies the meaning of dependent origination through impermanence,
and not anything else.
It is solely by virtue of the existence of conditions that the resultant dharma comes to exist;
it is not that the conditions possess a real, functional activity capable of producing the resultant dharma.
Nor is it established that a small amount of production occurs because a non-productive dharma serves as its cause.
The two types—non-action and impermanence—are the conditions;
it is not other types, such as active function and the unarisen dharma, that serve as the causes.
Therefore, it is said that "it is not others."

This distinguishes [the term] from [the notion of] Īśvara and others who possess real causal activity, as well as those who posit the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) as the condition for dependent origination, thereby explaining its name.
"Repeatedly ceasing and again arising in succession" refers to this.
It is called "dependent origination" (*pratītyasamutpāda*) because it arises continuously whenever conditions are encountered.
Regarding the phrase "having awakened to the nature of conditions in the past, they arise in equal succession":

after first realizing the nature of conditions at the time of attaining enlightenment, one subsequently gives rise to speech for the sake of sentient beings and explains it; therefore, it is called dependent origination.
Self-benefit is termed the "condition," while benefiting others is termed the "arising.
This refers to the meaning of the Dharma-wheel being transmitted in succession.
Within the eighth [category], the nature of the condition, there are two [aspects].
The *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* states that there are four conditions and two causes;
when the various members [of dependent origination] are considered in relation to one another, their predominance (*adhipatipratyaya*) is certainly present.
The existence or non-existence of the remaining three conditions is not fixed;
in the *Pratītyasamutpāda-sūtra*, based on their definitive existence, it is stated that there is only one—
namely, the dominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*).
Craving has the sense of being a causal condition for grasping, and becoming has the sense of being a causal condition for birth.
If it is said that the link of consciousness is the seed of karma, then volitional formations also act as a causal condition for consciousness.
The other members [of dependent origination], when viewed in relation to one another, lack the sense of being "causal conditions" (*nidāna*).
As for the *Abhidharmasamuccaya* stating that ignorance (*avidyā*) is a causal condition for volitional formations (*saṃskāra*),
this is said with reference to the karmic latencies (*vāsanā*) of ignorance.
Because it is associated with ignorance (*avidyā*), it is metaphorically designated as "ignorance," though in reality it is a type of formative action (*saṃskāra*).
A passage from this text states:
"The *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* says that when the various members [of dependent origination] are considered in relation to one another, there are none that do not function as causes and conditions."
According to the explanation that craving (*tṛṣṇā*) and grasping (*upādāna*) depend solely on karma-existence (*karmabhava*),
a specific analysis states: ignorance (*avidyā*) is,

in relation to formations (*saṃskāra*), and craving in relation to grasping, as well as birth (*jāti*) in relation to aging-and-death (*jarāmaraṇa*), both an immediately preceding condition (*samanantarapratyaya*) and an object-condition (*ālambanapratyaya*).
This refers to the case where an immaterial factor is considered in relation to another immaterial factor;
there exists a condition as an object (ālambana-pratyaya), but not as an immediately preceding condition (samanantara-pratyaya).
This refers to the case where a material factor is considered in relation to an immaterial factor.
In the case of the remaining members, both [the cause and the effect] are absent when viewed in relation to one another;
this text provides a general statement,
while that text provides a specific explanation.
It should be explained as follows:
regarding "form in relation to form," this refers to the form within name-and-form (nāmarūpa) in relation to the five sense bases (āyatana).
The arising of form is dependent upon karma;
the aging and death of form are dependent upon the arising of form.
As for the case where the formless is dependent upon the possessed-of-form: [it is likewise].
Ignorance in relation to volitional formations;
name in relation to the five bases;
and birth in the formless realm in relation to aging and death.
In this context, non-karmic existence (*abhavika*) is not mentioned; therefore, it is not discussed here.
Furthermore, this explanation is based on the immediate, sequential, and unconfused actual process of dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*).
When these are viewed in relation to one another, their functioning as conditions is not fixed;
those who are wise should reflect upon this according to reason.
As for the answer: "The causal condition (hetu-pratyaya) is that which is manifested by its own essential seed-condition."
The intent of this response is as follows:
regarding causes and conditions, the seed of ignorance gives rise only to ignorance and not to other links;
when each link is considered in relation to itself and not in relation to other links, this is precisely "dependent origination by way of intrinsic nature" (*svabhāva-pratītyasamutpāda*).
Now, the meaning of dependent origination regarding the pleasant and the unpleasant is explained.
This is said because, when self and other are viewed in relation to one another, there is the condition of predominance (*adhipati-pratyaya*) but no cause-condition (*hetu-pratyaya*).
As for the question, "Why is it said that dependent origination is established based on the essential nature of cause and effect? and so forth:
The intent of the question here is: since causes function through all four conditions, why is there no "causal condition" (hetu-pratyaya)?

The intent of the answer here is that although the causal condition exists within the ten types of causes—namely, among the producing, drawing forth, arising, specific, concurrent, and non-contradictory causes—it does not exist [as a distinct category] elsewhere.
The specific causes for their distinct natures, their production of a common function, their non-contradictory essence, and their pervasive yet remote relationship are not discussed here in detail.
Regarding the terms "inducing," "attracting," and "arising," there must be causal conditions for defining their names and explaining their meanings.
However, it is designated as an "inducing cause" (āvāhaka-hetu) only in reference to the mutual relationship between active manifestations (*samudācāra*).

Since this is explained in terms of karmic latencies (*vāsanā*) within the states of formations (*saṃskāra*) and existence (*bhava*), whether moistened or unmoistened, it is a dominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*) rather than a causal condition (*hetu-pratyaya*).

It does not preclude the sense that the seeds of craving (*tṛṣṇā-bīja*) are the causal condition (*hetu-pratyaya*) for the seeds of grasping (*upādāna*) in relation to birth, aging, and death, acting as their productive cause (*āvāhaka-hetu*).

Nor does it preclude the fact that, during the stage prior to being moistened [by craving], the five factors beginning with consciousness (*vijñāna*) act as the projecting cause (*ākṣepa-hetu*) for birth, aging, and death.

Once moistened, the five factors within the intermediate existence—consciousness and so forth—are the causes for arising in relation to birth and old age and death; thus, they possess the sense of being causal conditions (*nidāna*).
Because the referents [of "cause" and "condition"] are distinct, there is no contradiction.
Regarding the two causes:
Question—how many members are subsumed under the two types of causal results, namely those that project (*ākṣepa*) and those that produce (*abhinirvṛtti*)?

Answer—within the present life and the subsequent life, those members beginning with consciousness and ending with feeling, which are subsumed under the stages of birth (*jāti*) and aging-and-death (*jarāmaraṇa*).
This explains that the consciousness-link (vijñāna-aṅga), as the continuity of rebirth, consists of both the projecting cause and the projected result existing simultaneously.
Both are termed "projecting causes" because they are distant from their results;
however, the productive [cause] and the [result] that yields its fruit belong to different time periods.
That which is proximate and capable of producing [an effect] alone is called the "cause of production.
The *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* states:
"That which is proximate to and directly produces a fruit is termed the 'cause of production.'"
The "projecting cause" (*ākṣepa-hetu*) is so named because it projects a remaining fruit from afar.
The three natures and ten causes are as explained in other chapters;
since this discussion concerns defilement (*saṃkleśa*), it does not contradict other teachings.
In the ninth section, "Analysis of Conditions," there are thirty topical headings used for analysis.
The first is the analysis through questioning each individual link.
Regarding the two questions and answers concerning ignorance (*avidyā*):

as for the statement that "it is solely the cause for non-interruption," improper mental attention (*ayoniśomanasikāra*) acts as the cause for the non-interruption of ignorance, but it cannot act as the cause for defilement (*saṃkleśa*).
Because its essence is not defiled.
What is it that arises without the application of improper attention (*ayoniśo-manasikāra*) yet functions as dependent origination?
Therefore, it is called the cause of non-interruption, not the cause of defilement.
Regarding this, there are two interpretations of the passage. One says:
"Improper mental attention" refers to incorrect reflection associated with present ignorance.
This is because defilement cannot defile that which is already defiled by ignorance; therefore, it is not stated to be the cause of ignorance.
Second, it is said:
this is the attention associated with past ignorance.
Question: If that is so, past attention (manasikāra) coexists with ignorance (avidyā).
Why, then, do you say only that attention acts as the cause for the non-interruption of ignorance, and not that past ignorance acts as the cause for the non-interruption of present ignorance?
Answer: Although ignorance exists, it is not mentioned because its power is weak;
rather, the question and answer are formulated based on the strength of the power of attention (*manasikāra*).
Furthermore, as for the nature of this attention:
The two commentators provide the following explanations: one says it is "universal attention" (*sarvatraga-manasikāra*);
the other says: [it is]...
It is also included among the omnipresent mental factors (*sarvatraga-citta-saṃprayukta*).
Furthermore, regarding the phrase "impelled by the power of karma and afflictions that produce the defilement of birth":
this means that the defilement of birth arises from the defilement of karma.
The defilement of karma arises from the defilement of afflictions;
therefore, it is said to be "perfumed and activated" by them.
The essence of karma refers to the formative forces (*saṃskāra*).
The primary cause has ignorance (*avidyā*) as its essence.

Although all afflictions (*kleśa*) serve as causes for the initial arising of karma, ignorance alone is specifically mentioned because it possesses eleven superior characteristics, namely: being the object-condition (*ālambana*), and so forth.
As explained at length in the sūtras,
the *Abhidharmakośa* states:
"Ignorance is not said to have a cause."
Birth and death must have a beginning;
old age and death do not state a cause.
Birth and death must have an end.
From afflictions arise afflictions and karma;
from karma arises the objective entity;
from the objective entity arise further entities and afflictions.
Since the principle of the links of existence (*bhavāṅga*) is solely this,
the twelve links constitute a beginningless cycle of saṃsāra.
Pū-que (Supplement) says:
The essence of the defilement of birth is defiled by two conditions: karma and afflictions;
the cause of karma is defiled by the single condition of afflictions.
Therefore, that which is produced is called initial ignorance (*avidyā*).
Ignorance arises not because it is defiled by attention (*manasikāra*);
therefore, improper attention is not stated to be its causal origin.
Question: Why is it not stated that the very essence of ignorance serves as its own causal condition?
Answer: Because the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of ignorance, if it does not encounter other conditions, cannot increase or decrease its own defilement;
therefore, its own nature is not a condition.
Regarding the formations (*saṃskāra*), there are three questions and answers.
Because one does not comprehend that the cause of conventional suffering consists of non-meritorious formations (*apuṇyābhisaṃskāra*) and so forth conditioned by dependent origination,
the characteristics of suffering in the three miserable destinies are easily known as conventional suffering.
The suffering of the realms of humans and devas is subtle, hidden, and difficult to comprehend; it is known as "ultimate suffering" (paramārtha-duḥkha) by those possessing noble wisdom (āryajñāna).
Alternatively, some explain that among the eight types of suffering, the Abhidharma treatises designate the first seven as "conventional suffering" (saṃvṛti-duḥkha).
The eighth suffering is called ultimate suffering (*paramārtha-duḥkha*).
If one explains it in this way,
the eighth— suffering of conditioned existence (*saṃskāra-duḥkha*)— pervades all five destinies.
One should also give rise to meritorious and immovable karma while being deluded only regarding the miserable realms (*durgati*).
Since the first seven types of suffering apply to both humans and devas,
one should also create non-meritorious karma while being deluded only regarding the happy realms (*sugati*).

Because the suffering of suffering (*duḥkha-duḥkhatā*), the suffering of change (*vipariṇāma-duḥkhatā*), and the suffering of conditioned formations (*saṃskāra-duḥkhatā*) pertain to all five destinies (*gati*),
it is known from this that the previous explanation is correct.
Those [three types of] conventional and ultimate suffering are taught based on their respective distinctions of being coarse or subtle, and easy or difficult to know.
This general characteristic of the basis for suffering in terms of the conventional and the ultimate is taught as the object of experience for both ordinary beings and noble ones;
thus, it is not contradictory [to say that] there are meritorious and immovable karmas.
The immediate motivating cause (*samanantara-samutthāna*) consists solely of proximate wholesome volition (*kuśala-cetanā*).
The remote motivating cause (*dūre-samutthāna*) is initiated by ignorance (*avidyā*);
because one is deluded regarding the future fruit, delusion (*moha*) is said to be its condition.
If non-meritorious karma also has ignorance as its proximate cause,
it is because one is deluded regarding the future fruit.
To this, the answer is that within this context, the conditions for meritorious, non-meritorious, and immovable karma are explained in general terms.
The three unwholesome roots produce only non-merit;
the unwholesome root of delusion, however, extends to both merit and the imperturbable.
Thus, the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* states:
There exists an inferior ignorance that can give rise to superior formations;
otherwise, the higher meditative absorption (dhyāna) produced by one who has first suppressed the defilements of a lower stage would not constitute the limb of formations,
because the ignorance of that [higher] stage has not yet arisen.
Therefore, the unwholesome root of delusion universally gives rise to the three types of karma.
Question: Regarding the arousal of karma, there is the distinction between the primary factor and the auxiliary;

regarding the statement that the primary factor exists while the auxiliary does not, it is said that for the moistening of rebirth, there is the primary factor and the auxiliary, whereas for the primary factor itself, there is no auxiliary factor.

Answer: Since a single cause does not require extensive explanation and lacks the capacity for direct assistance, while auxiliary conditions necessarily depend upon a specific number, both the primary and the auxiliary are presented together.
As for the statement "based on the conditions that give rise to all practices," it is said as follows:
Not only is it because [the sūtra] speaks of the conditions for bodily and vocal actions that it does not state volition (*cetanā*) to be the condition for body and speech;
furthermore, because it speaks based on the conditions for the arising of wholesome and defiled volitions,
it states ignorance (*avidyā*) as a condition but does not state neutral (*avyākṛta*) formations as a condition.
Because the two courses of action— body and speech— are exclusively indeterminate (*avyākṛta*),
it is said that ignorance alone gives rise to the various formations (*saṃskāra*).
Furthermore, [ignorance] is proximate to the arousal of the three types of wholesome, afflicted, and indeterminate actions of body, speech, and mind.
The *Bùquè* says:
Although volition gives rise to the two courses of action—bodily and vocal—it does not itself give rise to volition;
rather, ignorance universally gives rise to all karmas.
Therefore, it is said only that ignorance conditions volitional formations (*saṃskāra*).
Furthermore, the three types of karma have volition (*cetanā*) as their essential nature;
when ignorance conditions volitional formations, wholesome and unwholesome volitions arise.
Therefore, it is not said that volition is the condition for formations (*saṃskāra*).

As for the answer, "Formations are the conditions for the defilement of consciousness (*vijñāna*) because they can project and produce the fruit of future existence," this means that formations can project the seeds of present consciousness and can produce the actual manifestation (*samudācāra*) of consciousness in a future existence.
It is not as if name-and-form alone can produce consciousness merely by serving as the sense-faculties and their objects.
Regarding the response that "consciousness can serve as the cause for its new arising," this is because consciousness enters the womb and acts as the cause for new birth.
Because the collective retribution can serve as the condition for specific retribution;
or because the seed of consciousness acts as the immediate cause for name-and-form, causing it to arise anew.
This explains the initial linking of rebirth of name-and-form.
In accordance with the principle that the lower consciousness enters the womb,
the previous explanation is correct.
Furthermore, this is stated based on all births and the moment of birth for all who are born.
At the time of taking birth through any of the four modes of birth or within any of the three realms of existence, the element of consciousness (vijñānadhātu) is invariably present; therefore,
consciousness alone is specifically mentioned,
whereas the other five [aggregates] are not so fixed.
Therefore, it is not mentioned.

Furthermore, regarding the statement that "because the six sense bases are preeminent and because the two types [of contact] are subsumed by the six sense bases," this refers only to the time when the six sense bases give rise to contact.
Regarding the statement, "This is categorized as such; the six bases and the six consciousnesses also give rise to contact,
because contact is their proximate cause," the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* says:
This means that the aspect of the desirable and so forth grasped by contact is proximate and adjacent to the aspect of appropriation and so forth grasped by feeling;
because it induces a superior [result],
through the power of feeling and so forth, one seeks either union with or separation from a corresponding object.
This means that the object of feeling and the object of craving are similar:
toward the object of pleasant feeling, one craves for union;
toward the object of painful feeling, one craves for separation.
It is called a "similar object.
Therefore, it is said that craving has the branch of feeling as its condition.
Ignorance merely fails to know, as they truly are, the characteristics of arising and ceasing regarding both internal and external feelings.
When one is unable to restrain the mind and gives rise to uncomprehending modes of activity,
craving that is neither intimate nor compliant is not said to function as a condition.
However, if it arises from a remote state due to delusion, even such craving possesses the sense of being a condition for the arising of feeling.
It is not because feeling is more intimate that feeling alone is said to be the condition for craving;
rather, it is because [craving] arises from longing that, at the time of pursuit, it can give rise to latent dispositions (*anuśaya*).
This is because craving seeks the union with desirable objects and the separation from undesirable ones.
Furthermore, the perfumed seeds give rise to the acquisition of latent tendencies (*anuśaya*) and induce the factors conducive to the arising of acquisition;
thus, acquisition brings about birth.
Therefore, it is stated specifically that craving is the condition for grasping.
Question: It was previously stated that ignorance serves as the condition for initiating karmic existence (*bhava*) and so forth.
Are both wholesome and unwholesome karmas—whether already moistened by craving or not yet moistened—designated as "existence"?
Because they are capable of producing results.
However, it is only after being moistened that they are able to approach the production of results and thus uniquely receive the name [saṃskāra].
Prior to being moistened, the initial formation—which is not yet augmented—is designated as "volitional formations" (saṃskāra).
Based on their distinct meanings, each receives its own name;
however, here, based on the general sense, it is said that ignorance gives rise to karmic existence (*karma-bhava*),
which is precisely *saṃskāra*.

However, at the stage of moistening, it is by the power of grasping (*upādāna*) that those very karmas are enabled to project the fruits of consciousness, name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*), and so forth, in their respective places of birth;
therefore, it is specifically said that grasping conditions becoming (*bhava*).
Regarding the second section, the Gate of the Three Paths:
according to the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi*, ignorance (*avidyā*),
craving (*tṛṣṇā*), and grasping (*upādāna*) are subsumed under the category of afflictions (*kleśa*).
These are precisely those three.
As for conduct, one part is subsumed under karma;
these are precisely those two.
That commentary states:
"Where it is said that karma completely encompasses existence (bhava),
one should know that this is spoken with reference to karmic existence (karma-bhava)."

Regarding the statement in the *Abhidharmakośabhāṣya* that "in some places it is said that consciousness is subsumed under karma," that refers to the seeds of karma being designated as the limb of consciousness (*vijñāna-aṅga*).
Regarding the phrase "the rest are the path to suffering":
by this standard, it means that the remaining seven branches are collectively designated as "existence" because they constitute the paths of karma.
The *Cheng weishi lun* (Treatise on the Establishment of Consciousness-Only) states:
"The seventh [consciousness] has one part that is subsumed under suffering,
because the five types of consciousness and so forth are called 'existence' (*bhava*) when they undergo transformation."
The third section, the analysis of cause and effect, has two parts.
First, it establishes cause and effect based on the sequential relationship of the twelve links.
Second, it states that three [links] are exclusively causes.
Because ignorance, craving, and grasping are the roots that initiate karma and moisten rebirth;
the two that are exclusively results are birth and old age and death.
Because this is the fruit produced by the ten preceding members,
and because it is further distinguished by its dependence on the three types of affliction (*saṃkleśa*) and the causal relationship between seeds and manifestations,
there are briefly five levels when the factors of dependent origination are collectively categorized as cause and fruit.
First, the gate of origination (*samutthāna-mukha*):
this refers to the preceding serving as cause and the succeeding serving as effect.
It is precisely these initial statements—such as "the first is solely cause" and so forth—that constitute this.
Regarding the two aspects of root and branch, cause and effect:
this second passage is [the one that addresses] the root,
because afflictions constitute the root.
The three [links] are exclusively causes and so forth.
Below this it is also stated:
"The preceding six branches, as well as craving, grasping, and existence, constitute the causal division."
The latter two members constitute the fruit-portion.
Feeling (vedanā) pertains to both types;
thus, cause and effect are distinguished according to their fundamental and derivative aspects.
Regarding the three types of results— those that are maturation, those that are not maturation, and cause-and-effect [results]—

the *Pañcavastuka-vibhāṣā-śāstra* (Treatise on the Five Categories) states: "Furthermore, the five members comprised within the present result and the two members comprised within the future result are collectively termed 'dependent origination subsumed under results'."
One should know that the remaining members are dependent origination subsumed under causes.
The *Madhyāntavibhāga*, first fascicle, also states:
"That which is defiled by causes refers to the categories of afflictions and karma."
Resultant defilement refers to the remaining portions:
the causes and results of the four types of maturation, whether matured or immature.
As the Abhidharma-śāstra states:
At the time of the cause, there are the "projecting" and the "projected," which are the aforementioned seven members.
At the time of the fruit, there are the "producing" and the "produced," namely the latter five members.
This is because, through the maturation of ignorance, craving and grasping arise, and by their increase, [the subsequent members follow].
Because the six factors beginning with formations (saṃskāra) are matured, they are termed "existence" (bhava);
thus, the two factors of birth (jāti) and old age-and-death (jarāmaraṇa) are that which is matured.
This constitutes the causal relationship between five stages.
Regarding the statement in the preceding section on the two causes that induce [rebirth]:
"The inducing cause and the producing cause together comprise ten members, which are termed the cause;
the final two members are the result."
The *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* also states:
"The ten causes and two fruits are necessarily not of the same time period.
Although various sections explain them with five different meanings, [they all agree on this point].
While the expectations differ, the underlying principle does not contradict itself.
Fourth, the clarification of the characteristics of the distinct and the mixed:
the third [point] concerns the characteristics of the distinct, and so forth.
The *Cheng weishi lun* (Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi-śāstra) states:
"Ignorance (*avidyā*), craving (*tṛṣṇā*), and grasping (*upādāna*) are called 'unique characteristics' (*kevala-lakṣaṇa*),
because they do not intermingle with other members [of dependent origination]."
The others are the mixed characteristics (*miśralakṣaṇa*).
That is to say, when the meaning of a preceding or succeeding factor is fixed and does not shift to become the name of another member, it is called a distinct characteristic (*kevalalakṣaṇa*);
that which is contrary to this is a mixed characteristic.
That which is capable of inducing desirable or undesirable fruits is,
in its essence, the member of existence (*saṃskāra*);
for prior to being moistened [by craving], it is designated as the "inducing cause" (*ākṣepa-hetu*).
As for that which can produce the differentiation of destinies,
it refers to the limb of existence (*bhava*).
It is called "existence" because the formative forces (*saṃskāra*) are moistened and set in motion by it.
Because they are capable of producing the [subsequent] members:
the fact that consciousness and a portion of name-and-form and the six sense bases possess mixed characteristics means,
for instance, that at the stage of the member of consciousness, all five aggregates are present.
However, it is only consciousness that is designated as a link;
therefore, it constitutes a single part.
Upon reaching the stage of name-and-form, consciousness transforms into "name."
It is designated as one part [of the six internal bases].
When it reaches the stage of the six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*), consciousness (*vijñāna*) further transforms and is designated as the mind base (*manāyatana*), and not the other five bases;
this too is one part.
However, although the nature of consciousness is one, it passes through the three branches with different names in succession;
since their meanings also differ,
they are called "mixed characteristics."
Because contact and feeling are not consciousness, they are not mixed with it;
that which pertains to the time of defilement is the member of consciousness.
This refers to what was stated in the preceding text.
Due to wrong conduct, the mind becomes inverted;
when this inverted manifesting consciousness perfumes seeds,
it is then called the "consciousness link" (vijñāna-aṅga).
Regarding the stage of moistening:
the seed of consciousness is moistened by craving and grasping;
at the initial moment of linking rebirth, it is termed the limb of name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*).
Regarding the stage of evolution:
when this name-and-form (nāmarūpa) gives rise to the six sense faculties (ṣaḍāyatana), it is termed the limb of the six sense bases (ṣaḍāyatanāṅga).
It is not the case that the six sense bases and so forth are entirely nothing but consciousness (vijñāna).
Because all possess consciousness,
they are thus mixed.
As for the phrase "because it specifically reveals the characteristic of suffering," etc.:
Now, the present consciousness and its concomitants arise as five branches to repay the preceding causes;
these five branches manifest clearly,
specifically revealing the characteristic of suffering.
If dharmas that are of the same maturation as those in the future have not yet manifested,
they are collectively termed "birth and death" (*saṃsāra*).
This birth and death consists of one [factor] in the present, which is projected by the seven projecting causes, beginning with ignorance (*avidyā*).
The second [link], craving and grasping, serves as the cause for the three types of existence (*bhava*).
Because it is produced from that cause, and because it reveals the distinction between projecting (*ākṣepa*) and actualizing (*abhinirvṛtti*),
this birth and old age and death arise in the present when the body of the subsequent birth manifests.
There is a slight difference in the expansion;
it is divided into five branches.
Therefore, it is said that this separately reveals the characteristic of suffering.
It should be understood that in this system, the five members beginning with present consciousness and the two future members have overlapping characteristics:
the member of birth fully encompasses the five members beginning with consciousness,
whereas old age and death encompass only the latter portion of the member of existence.
Therefore, it is called "having mixed characteristics.
Alternatively, the five factors—consciousness and the others—which exist together with old age and death as they moisten rebirth, are also said to have mixed characteristics.
This is the fifth time the meaning of the term "dependent origination" (pratītyasamutpāda) is explained within the Sūtra.
In Sanskrit it is *pratītya*, which here means "should be practiced," because there is no abiding.
In Sanskrit it is *sam*, which here means "conjunction."
Because it is a correct collection;
"uṭ" in Sanskrit is translated here as "arising," because it arises based on conditions.
Among these three meanings, the first provides a general explanation of "dependent origination" (pratītyasamutpāda) to distinguish it from the unconditioned;
the second explains only the character "condition" (prati) to show that conditions do not deviate;
and the third explains only the character "arising" (samutpāda) to distinguish it from dharmas that do not arise.
As explained in detail in the *Nyāyānusāra*.
Regarding "dependent origination" (*pratītyasamutpāda*) and "dependently arisen" (*pratītyasamutpanna*),
if one follows the *Abhidharma*, it says:
The cause is called "dependent origination" (pratītyasamutpāda) and the result is called "dependently arisen" (pratītyasamutpanna).
Within the sixth [section], which subsumes the Four Noble Truths,
it is stated that these seven branches are all the Truth of Suffering (duḥkhasatya).
Having finished explaining that the remaining five factors are exclusively the truth of origination (*samudaya-satya*),
this is done to reveal the distinction in essence between the two truths;
it is not that all five factors are entirely the truth of origination.
The *Cheng weishi lun* (Treatise on the Establishment of Consciousness-Only) states:
"Because they are all comprised within the nature of the aggregates as the truth of suffering (*duḥkhasatya*),
the five [aggregates] are also comprised within the truth of origination (*samudayasatya*)."
Because they are of the nature of karma and afflictions,
being oppressed is the meaning of suffering;
thus, all things are suffering.
Because they summon maturation (*vipāka*) and because they possess the meaning of accumulation (*cita*),
the five [aggregates] are also the truth of accumulation (*samudaya-satya*).
Regarding the seven factors as they relate to one another within the context of the three conditions,
there are sixteen rounds of question and answer;
these concern such statements as "due to ignorance regarding the dharmas that accord with the formative forces (*saṃskāra*)," and so forth.
Master Ki explains:
Unwholesome mental formations are called "conformable formations" because they arise simultaneously with ignorance as their momentary origination (*kṣaṇasamutthāna*).
It is called "concomitant with obscuration" because it is associated with ignorance that is unrestrained by the five wrong views and characterized by heedlessness;
this is because it arises conditioned by those views rather than being directly conditioned by the formative forces (*saṃskāra*).
Unwholesome conduct of body and speech serves as the immediately preceding condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*).

Alternatively, ignorance associated with the view of a self-identity (*satkāya-dṛṣṭi*) and other such views serves as the immediately preceding condition that directly induces the various formations (*saṃskāra*).
As for wholesome conduct, it is induced by ignorance as a remote condition (*parokṣa-pratyaya*).
Because one first gives rise to the two initial volitions through delusion regarding that fruit, and only subsequently initiates the formative activities (*saṃskāra*),
the establishment of a future fruit based on a condition that has long since ceased is accomplished.
This explains how the distinction between the two types of formative activities brings about the fruit.
It can also serve as a co-existent condition (*sahabhū-pratyaya*) for wholesome conduct;
however, because it is not the primary initiator of karma at the moment of its arising (*kṣaṇa-samutthāna*), it is not mentioned here.
Such meanings should be understood by applying these principles accordingly.
Regarding this, two Western commentators state:
"The untainted [states] of the two vehicles are also accompanied by ignorance."
How much more so for contaminated wholesome [karma].
According to this principle, wholesome karma such as merit can coexist with ignorance and likewise takes ignorance as its simultaneous condition (*sahabhū-pratyaya*).
The second [interpretation] states:
"Because wholesome and unwholesome karma coexist with ignorance.
This passage generally treats ignorance in relation to volitional formations as three conditions.
To distinguish between the wholesome and the unwholesome:
the unwholesome has three conditions, whereas the wholesome lacks such simultaneous conditions.
Therefore, while the words of this treatise are general, their intended meaning is specific.
Regarding the fact that formations serve as three conditions for consciousness:
because formations simultaneously perfume and activate the seeds of consciousness,
they constitute the co-existent condition (*sahabhū-pratyaya*).
Through the power of volitional formations (*saṃskāra*), the seeds of consciousness (*vijñāna*) in the subsequent moments continue to grow;
this is the condition of immediate cessation (*anantara-nirodha*).
By means of those seeds of formation, the fruit of future consciousness is brought into arising.
This refers to conditions that have ceased long ago.
Regarding how sensation (vedanā) serves as three types of conditions for craving (tṛṣṇā):
it acts as a co-existent condition (sahabhū-pratyaya), among others, by virtue of craving arising simultaneously with the manifest activity of sensation.

Regarding the statement that craving (*tṛṣṇā*) and grasping (*upādāna*) are coexistent because they proceed together with attachment (*lobha*), and that one establishes a desire for those phenomena conducive to grasping—
craving and the act of grasping are, in reality, not simultaneous.
The objects grasped and the causes and conditions for grasping coexist with craving (*tṛṣṇā*).
In relation to grasping (*upādāna*), craving constitutes a coexistent condition (*sahabhū-pratyaya*).

In relation to becoming (*bhava*), grasping functions as three types of conditions; furthermore, it acts as a remote condition (*dūre-pratyaya*) by activating the functional capacity for that realm over a long duration.
This refers to the self-love at the moment of birth as distinct from its subsequent continuity;
because the self-love at the point of death is separated from the initial arising in the various realms by the single moment of actual death,
it constitutes a long-term condition.
Regarding the three conditions for the prospect of rebirth, it is said that "that which perfumes and awakens those seeds" means:
once the seeds of karma belonging to the branch of existence (*bhava-aṅga*) have been moistened,

they act as the co-existent condition (*sahabhū-pratyaya*) by supporting and awakening the seeds of designation (*nāma-kāya*) such as consciousness (*vijñāna*), thereby causing birth (*jāti*) and so forth to arise.
Master Ki says: Because seeds such as consciousness have been perfumed by past karma, they are now termed "existence" (bhava);
and because they produce manifest results, they constitute "simultaneous existence" (sahabhū).
Thus, even though [the cause] has long since ceased, the result continues to evolve.
Just as a moist seed has the expectation of initial germination,
because the fruit transforms, it becomes a remote cessation that acts as an inducing condition (*ākṣepaka-pratyaya*),
since it is separated from the moment of actual death.
Eighth, regarding the discernment of the branches of existence (bhavāṅga) in terms of their predominant and complete aspects:
there are two ways of establishing these branches—
first, the predominant aspect, and second, the complete aspect.
At the beginning, there is only karma as existence (*bhava*).
Later, the six [bases] constitute existence.
Because they are moistened by grasping (*upādāna*), they are further designated as "existence" and termed "appropriation" (*parigraha*).
The ninth section on the function of karma has two parts:
first, clarifying the extent of karmic activity;
second, clarifying the breadth or narrowness of its conditions.
Regarding these very functional activities and the respective activities appropriate to each individual sphere of operation,
the Abhidharma treatises state that the factor of ignorance has two kinds of functions.
First, it causes sentient beings to be deluded regarding existence;
second, it serves as the condition for volitional formations (*saṃskāra*).
Thus, up to birth, there are two kinds of karma.
First, they cause the arising of name-and-form and so forth for all sentient beings;
second, they act as conditions for aging and death.
Thus, each of these members possesses two functions.
That which is the second karma refers here to the very function of this karma.
It concerns the three types of conditions mentioned in the preceding text and all the karmic activities within their respective objects.
That is precisely what constitutes the first karma.
It is said that old age and death also have two types of karma:
first, they repeatedly cause the temporal stages of sentient beings to change, thereby destroying their youth and vigor.
Second, because they cause the lifespan of sentient beings to undergo change and destroy that lifespan.
In this context, it is stated that only the preceding member serves as a condition for the succeeding one; therefore, there is no "condition for old age and death" [outside of birth].
There is no contradiction.
The analysis of conditions as being broad, narrow, or intermediate consists of three parts.
First, the meaning of distant and proximate conditions is clarified.
Second, it clarifies that the latter is not the condition for the former.
Third, it concludes [the section].
Tenth, it explains the scriptural passage: "Because this exists, that exists," and so forth.
First, it reveals that dependent origination is without activity;
it is solely by virtue of the existence of conditions that resultant phenomena come to exist,
for conditions do not possess a real activity capable of producing resultant phenomena.
The statement means that because [the cause] has not been severed, it possesses the sense of arising from other conditions.
Second, it reveals that dependent origination is impermanent;
for a produced phenomenon cannot be established by taking a non-arising phenomenon as its cause.
The latter two clarify the meaning of the arising of power and function;
that is to say, although all phenomena are without agency (the third point),
and although all phenomena are impermanent (the fourth point).
However, it is not the case that all effects arise by taking any single phenomenon as their condition;
rather, such a statement is made because of the distinct functional capacities of various phenomena.
Alternatively, this first [point] refutes the notion of "conditioned arising through activity."
The second refutes the [view of] dependent origination as permanent.
The third reveals the dependent origination of dynamic efficacy.
The fourth refutes the dependent origination of unequal conditions, which would entail the fallacy that another performs the action while I receive the fruit.
Within the eleven four-line [verses] and other such classifications,
these are not necessarily constituent members;
they are mentioned there in a general sense.
In the second clause regarding ignorance, the fact that it is an obscured-unspecified karma with a distinct retribution-result is not mentioned because it is abbreviated.
The same applies to the second clause regarding formations, where the fact that consciousness is also obscured-unspecified is not mentioned.

There may be cases where craving exists but is not conditioned by feeling; this refers to the craving for the seeking of liberation and the craving based on wholesome desire that leads one to abandon other forms of craving.
This "wholesome desire for the Dharma" is frequently termed the craving for liberation.
Furthermore, for one who has abandoned craving through all wholesome disenchantment,
the unpleasant does not arise conditioned by agreeable feeling,
because at that time— and prior to it— there is no feeling and no agreeable feeling to serve as a condition.
To say that it is not a condition is not contradictory;
in truth, one should follow the latter part of the statement here.
All that is craving necessarily arises conditioned by feeling.
However, there are instances where feeling serves as a condition but is not itself craving;
this refers to the subsequent remaining links [of dependent origination].
Regarding the twelve factors that obstruct the Eightfold Noble Path, all twelve links serve as obstacles to right view, right thought, and so forth.
