However, in this context, we speak of the predominant obstacles; thus, we mention only ignorance (*avidyā*), the defiled mental formations (*saṃskāra*), and the existence of mental formations as being obstacles to right view and the others.
The bodily formations, verbal formations, and one portion of form obstruct right speech and so forth;
excluding ignorance and formations, which obstruct them in their entirety, the remaining nine links and a small portion of one link obstruct right mindfulness and right concentration.
This statement regarding "the rest" refers to the complete exposition of the nine factors.
There are two interpretations of this:
first, it is said:
Since the first three branches are said to obstruct the body of wisdom (*prajñāskandha*) and the body of ethical discipline (*śīlaskandha*),
the remaining nine branches are collectively termed "obstructions to right concentration" (*samyaksamādhi*) by extension.
In reality, however, it should be stated that only craving (*tṛṣṇā*) and grasping (*upādāna*) obstruct the path of detachment, mindfulness (*smṛti*), and concentration (*samādhi*).
The second says:
"The body of meditative concentration is the training of the mind;
the factor of consciousness is the mind."
Name-and-form, the six sense bases, birth, and old age and death— along with the mental substance— constitute the obstruction to meditative concentration and the body.
The two members of contact and feeling are mental concomitants (caitta),
as are name within [the category of] name-and-form, matter, and the first five sense bases.
In summary, consciousness constitutes the basis for the body of right concentration;
the two links of craving and grasping constitute the basis for the path of detachment.
This explains that right view, right thought, and right effort constitute the training in wisdom.
Right speech, right action, and right livelihood constitute the training in ethical discipline (śīla-śikṣā);
right mindfulness and right concentration constitute the training in meditative concentration (samādhi-śikṣā).
This is according to the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi-śāstra* (Cheng weishi lun) regarding the inclusion of the six pāramitās within the three trainings.
Some say that diligence is comprised within the three [trainings] because it universally governs all three;
others say that diligence is solely ethical discipline (*śīla*) because the discussion is based on the beginner.
Because of guarding the precepts,
it now relies on long-established practice;
since it is perfected through the assistance of diligence and because its vision is supreme, it is solely the body of wisdom (*prajñā-kāya*).
Because right mindfulness gives rise to the factors of right concentration,
it is subsumed under the training in concentration (*samādhi-śikṣā*);
for through mindfulness, there is clear recollection and the mind is focused with one-pointedness.
Among the thirteen gates of defilement and purity,
four belong exclusively to the category of total defilement;
these are ignorance, craving, grasping, and consciousness.
Question: It can be understood that the three afflictions are defiled;
why, however, is consciousness considered defiled?
Answer: As stated above, it is because of wrong practice that it causes the mind to become inverted.
Because the mind is inverted, this consciousness is defiled.
Since this is based on the final moment of consciousness in the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) as a link, it is said that four [links] are exclusively defiled.
Alternatively, the fourth [link] is the link of old age and death (*jarāmaraṇa*).
Because one is unable to practice and train during the stage of old age and death, these are designated as "defiled.
The five members beginning with consciousness are explained by analogy with the member of birth.
In reality, these six members are neither defiled nor pure.
The name "cause" is applied according to the fruits of both collective and individual karma.
The *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* states:
"The third [category] is exclusively defiled because its nature is that of affliction (*kleśa*)."
The seven [factors] are exclusively non-defiled because they are the fruit of maturation (*vipāka*).

Regarding this passage, it is stated that within the stages of these seven factors, defilement may arise; thus, they are metaphorically described as being common to both [the defiled and the non-defiled].
Because the others pertain to both [types],
these alone— being defiled— are said to consist of four members;
alternatively, consciousness or old age and death are metaphorically designated by the name "defiled."
The doctrine of Consciousness-Only (Vijñaptimātra), when considered according to reality, is likewise not contradictory.
Regarding the "gate where the cause perishes and the fruit is lost," there are three types of origination:
the envelopments (paryavasthāna), the latent dispositions (anuśaya), and ignorance (avidyā).
Master Ba said:
"Enveloping" refers to manifest ignorance,
while "latent tendency" refers to seed ignorance.
Initiation is precisely the initiation of karma.
Non-specific ignorance (āveṇikī-avidyā) pervades all three types.
Furthermore, another interpretation states:
There are three kinds of origination: the enveloping (*paryavasthāna*) and latent (*anuśaya*) ignorance of the three realms.
These are able to set the formative forces (*saṃskāra*) in motion;
because these [ignorances] are extinguished, the formative forces are also extinguished accordingly.
In the previous explanation, which followed the *Pratītyasamutpāda-sūtra*,
Master Ji stated that "initiation" refers to the ignorance that initiates karma (*karmābhisamskāra-avidyā*).
This [ignorance] is associated with the universal [defilements] and is not uncommon;
"enveloping" (paryavasthāna) refers to the ignorance that moistens rebirth,
which is for the most part only associated [with other mental factors].
When these two function together,
the seeds perfumed by them are called latent ignorance (*anuśaya-avidyā*).
This is because the ignorance that initiates action takes all forms of ignorance as its root.
In this context, it is explained in general that ignorance (avidyā) moistens rebirth;
furthermore, the formations (saṃskāra) correspond to becoming (bhava),
and ignorance corresponds to craving (tṛṣṇā) and grasping (upādāna).
Therefore, this is explained in general.
Furthermore, these three types of origination constitute the totality;
herein there are two.
That is to say, the outbursts (*paryavasthāna*) and the latent tendencies (*anuśaya*). Because they are discussed both collectively and individually, they are called the "three types.
As for the entities that initiate [defilement], the four—namely, the associated and the non-associated—are subsumed into three.
Because these three are collectively extinguished,
that specific ignorance which gives rise to volitional formations (*saṃskāra*) is extinguished;
because that is extinguished, volitional formations are extinguished.
This explanation comprehensively addresses the ignorance that initiates all formations (*saṃskāra*).
Otherwise, if it were not so, why would the ignorance that moistens rebirth (*upapatti-pratisaṃdhi*)—which has not yet been extinguished—be extinguished at the very moment it initiates formations?
Furthermore, there are three types of underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*) of ignorance that give rise to the envelopments (*paryavasthāna*).
First, it can give rise to the envelopments (*paryavasthāna*);
second, it can give rise to associated [defilements];
third, it can give rise to the unshared [defilements].
These three are all *paryavasthāna* (envelopments).
The first is general, while the latter two are specific.
There are three types of underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*) that give rise to these active manifestations of ignorance.
Because ignorance (*avidyā*) among these three latent tendencies (*anuśaya*) ceases, the active ignorance (*samudācāra-avidyā*) ceases;
because active ignorance ceases, the formative forces (*saṃskāra*) cease.

Regarding "the formative forces within one's own continuum that have already been performed and have ceased, as well as those for which an antidote has not yet arisen," Jing says: [this refers to] all formative forces within one's own continuum that have already been produced and have already ceased, and those that have not yet given rise to an antidote.
This refers to the fact that various formations (saṃskāra) have already been produced within one's own continuum and have not yet been abandoned.
Because these do not exist, consciousness (vijñāna) does not exist.
Furthermore, it is said that because mental formations (manasaḥ saṃskārāḥ) arise, bodily and vocal formations arise; because these exist, those exist.
From the activity of volition arise the activities of body and speech;
through volition, those [activities] of body and speech exist.
This specific mention of "existence" (bhava) serves to clarify "non-existence" (abhava).
Regarding the statement, "Because that does not exist, the consciousness conditioned by it also does not exist":
since those bodily formations and verbal formations do not exist, that consciousness also does not exist;
this is the correct sequential explanation.
As for the statement that if these were to be completely extinguished, consciousness would likewise follow in being extinguished:
when the three types of action— of body, speech, and mind— are completely extinguished,
consciousness likewise follows in being extinguished.
Master Ji’s commentary explains:
that which has already been performed and not yet extinguished within one's own continuum is called mental activity (*manas-karman*).
Furthermore, because of mental activity, there arise bodily and vocal activities; these are the two types of activity, namely bodily and vocal.
Regarding the statement, "By virtue of these three formations, consciousness exists;
because formations are absent, the consciousness conditioned by them is likewise absent," this means that the seed-consciousness takes formations as its condition.
Because formative forces (*saṃskāra*) are absent, consciousness (*vijñāna*) is absent.
If formative forces are entirely non-existent, that consciousness is also non-existent;
or, because this seed-consciousness is entirely non-existent, the manifest consciousness is also non-existent.

Regarding the statement that "the principle by which ignorance conditions volitional formations is likewise the principle by which craving conditions grasping and grasping conditions existence," Master Jing explains:
[He] asks, "The principle by which ignorance conditions volitional formations can be understood as being analogous to the principle by which grasping conditions existence."
In what way do they resemble craving as the condition for grasping?
The explanation says:
there is some slight resemblance, but it is not complete.
Just as unwholesome ignorance previously gives rise to volitional formations (*saṃskāra*) associated with subsequent unwholesome ignorance,
the principle that craving gives rise to grasping is the same. This does not, however,
refer to ignorance giving rise to other bodily, vocal, or mental formations, nor to the arising of meritorious or immovable formations.
Regarding the principle that because feeling does not exist, craving does not exist, and so on up to the principle that consciousness has volitional formations as its condition:
Jing says that this condition gives rise to craving through false pleasure,
just as erroneous cognition arises from improper conduct.
Therefore, they belong to the same category.
Master Ji says: [One might ask,] "Feeling (vedanā) is a fruit, while craving (tṛṣṇā) is an affliction (kleśa).
Volitional formations (saṃskāra) are karma, while consciousness (vijñāna) is a fruit."
They are not similar at all.
How can they be said to be analogous?
Answer: Because the activity (*saṃskāra*) and consciousness (*vijñāna*) differ in their karmic results, they are distinct when compared as different natures.
Now, although the afflictions that result in sensation and craving differ in nature, they are nonetheless of the same category; therefore, they are indicated as being non-distinct.
This is like how maturation arises from karma, and affliction arises from maturation;
because they belong to the same class, there is no contradiction in their meaning.
The Master’s commentary explains:
Just as with ignorance as a condition for volitional formations and consciousness as a condition, through their cessation, consciousness ceases;
likewise, with contact conditioned by ignorance as a condition for feeling and craving as a condition, through their cessation, craving ceases.
They are categorized as "types" because their meanings are similar.
Among the fifteen sets of eightfold gateways for the mutual inclusion of dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*),
three gateways are those manifested by that [dependent origination].
This is the general explanation.
Below follows the detailed analysis:

"One part of two" refers to the door of the arising of internal consciousness and the door of the performance of one's own karma; "one whole part" refers to what is manifested as the door of the revolving of the world of sentient beings.
The "Gate of the Arising of Internal Consciousness" (*jìngyún nèishí shēngmén*) refers only to the six sense organs giving rise to the six consciousnesses;
however, consciousness is subsumed under the member of consciousness (*vijñāna-aṅga*), and thus does not exhaust all members of dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*).

The "Gate of What is Accomplished by One's Own Karma" (*zìyè suǒzuò mén*) refers only to karma arising from volitional formations (*saṃskāra*) producing the distinctions among the five destinies (*pañca-gati*).
Because it does not include the seeds of the three afflictions and the five factors,
it does not fully encompass the members of existence (*bhavāṅga*).
For what reason are the other five gates not revealed by the twelve [members]?
This means that the doctrine of the twelve links of dependent origination clarifies the causes and effects within the internal body of sentient beings;

it does not concern the maturation of external crops or the formation and destruction of the vessel-world (bhājanaloka), as these are neither internal bodily causes and effects nor comprised within the twelve links.
The gate of sustenance by food refers solely to how external food nourishes sentient beings; it is not that the internal body itself can produce conditions.
The gate of majestic power clarifies reliance upon individual factors.

The five supernormal powers (pañcābhijñā) all arise based on the nine stages; because they have the sense of the supernormal power of the exhaustion of outflows (āsravakṣaya), they are not the twelve links of dependent origination.

As for the "gate of purification," this refers to the factors of enlightenment (bodhipākṣikadharma); since they are untainted (anāsrava) and arise from conditions, they likewise do not constitute the twelve branches of dependent origination.
Master Ji says: "The gateway of the arising of internal consciousness refers to consciousness arising based on the sense faculties;
this means that the various consciousnesses constitute the gateway of the essence.
Regarding the gateway of the performance of one's own karma, there are general and specific ways in which karma invites its maturation (*vipāka*)."
It is called "a portion" because it is merely a collective report.
There are three types of dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*): first, dependent origination by way of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).
That is to say, the eighth retributive consciousness is dependent origination as the nature of self-arising;
second, dependent origination as experience,
which refers to the six consciousnesses experiencing their respective objects.
The three types of craving arise conditioned by the paths of the agreeable and the disagreeable;
these are the twelve links.
The gateway for the arising of consciousness depends upon the sense faculties and their corresponding objects.
The "gate of experiencing what is produced by conditions" is precisely like dependent origination through experience;
the "gate of what is performed by one's own karma" is precisely like dependent origination through intrinsic nature.
The first is entirely the path of the agreeable and the disagreeable.

Furthermore, although the roots of goodness conducive to liberation (*mokṣabhāgīya*) and so forth are called "gateways to purification," they are nonetheless conditions that oppose and harm the process of transmigration (*saṃsāra*);
moreover, because they do not accord with or benefit it, they are also not included [within the categories of transmigration].
It contradicts the meaning of the process of saṃsāra,
as explained in the *Pratītyasamutpāda-sūtra*,
which distinguishes sixteen types of faults and benefits.
Regarding the five faults:
first, it gives rise to the view of a self;
second, it gives rise to the view of the past limit.
Third, the arising of views regarding the future limit;
fourth, the arising of views regarding both the past and future limits;
fifth, being intensely attached to those views with firm grasping and fear, and thus not attaining parinirvāṇa.
Master Ji says: "The first is the view of self (*ātma-dṛṣṭi*) as the root.
Based on this, there arise the views of annihilationism and eternalism regarding the three time periods, along with false views (*mithyā-dṛṣṭi*), making three.
Among the sixty-two views, according to their respective applications, they give rise to views of eternalism, annihilationism, and false views in relation to the three time periods."
The fifth is the intense and firm grasping of this very view as superior,
fearing that nirvāṇa will not be attained in the present life;

this is either the *dṛṣṭiparāmarśa* (clinging to views) or the *mithyādṛṣṭi* (wrong view) of those who propound the fivefold attainment of nirvāṇa in the present life (*pañca-dṛṣṭadharmanirvāṇavāda*).

The distinction between these two lies in the fact that one abides in the teachings and other such dharmas, while the other knows them according to their true meaning.
Regarding the four abidings:
because this nature of phenomena (dharmatā) is taught through unerring words and phrases,
those words and phrases capable of explaining it are called the "abiding of the Dharma" (dharma-sthiti).
Therefore, this abiding of phenomena (dharmasthiti) has the nature of phenomena (dharmatā) as its cause.
Consequently, this nature of phenomena is called the "dharma-realm" (dharmadhātu).
Here, "realm" (dhātu) carries the meaning of "cause" (hetu).
Alternatively, according to the meaning of the texts and the explanations in such sūtras as the *Prajñāpāramitā*, that True Suchness (*tathatā*) is named the "abiding of phenomena" (*dharmasthiti*).
Because that which is expressed [by the teachings] follows from the teaching, it is called the "abiding of phenomena.
Since it is the essence of the abiding of phenomena, there must first be the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*) before it can serve as the basis for the teaching.
Taking the substance as the cause and the meaning as the "element" (dhātu):
if the five types of arising were non-existent,
this would refer to the five links beginning with consciousness arising from seeds.
That which arises without location and without abiding may indeed exist;

In the preceding analysis of the twelve links,
why is it that while the other ten ancillary links do not serve as mutual conditions for one another,
name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*) and consciousness (*vijñāna*) alone are specifically established as being mutual conditions?
Regarding the answer that "consciousness uses name-and-form as its condition within the present life":
this means that because consciousness arises dependently upon what is conventionally designated as name-and-form at the stage of birth, it takes them as its condition.
Furthermore, regarding "it uses consciousness as its condition within the subsequent life": [this refers to how name-and-form take consciousness as their condition].
When name-and-form arises, it necessarily depends upon consciousness for its origination.
This explains that in the present, they serve as mutual conditions for one another;
specifically, the manifest name-and-form arises dependent upon consciousness.
When future consciousness arises, it likewise depends upon name-and-form.
Why is this? [The text] below thus interrogates and explains that they serve as mutual conditions for one another.
Regarding the statement that "the seven contemplations of the dark category (kṛṣṇapakṣa) extend only as far as the link of consciousness":
the two truths of suffering and its origin are called the dark category,
while the two truths of cessation and the path are called the white category (śuklapakṣa).
Regarding the teaching on the Chapter on Cessation:

because consciousness and name-and-form serve as mutual conditions for one another, one contemplates the mind back through to consciousness and then returns again to old age and death; therefore, it is called "reversal."
The manner of their cessation is as explained in the ninety-third [fascicle] and the preceding fascicle.
In the Chapter on Cessation (*nirodha-varga*), name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*) is not the cause for the cessation of consciousness;
it is not by the cessation of name-and-form that the factor of consciousness ceases.
However, because name-and-form necessarily cease when consciousness ceases,
one proceeds until reaching consciousness and further advances in contemplative practice even unto ignorance.
Because ignorance ceases, volitional formations (saṃskāra) accordingly cease.
Therefore, the contemplation is established through forty-four knowledges or seventy-seven knowledges;
since there are no causal links prior to ignorance,
forty-eight knowledges and so forth are likewise not mentioned.
The *Vibhāṣā* (40) states:
"In the stage where the Bodhisattva increases aversion toward conditioned formations (*saṃskāra*), he contemplates only up to consciousness (*vijñāna*).
Because he delights in the cessation [of suffering], he contemplates all twelve links."
Regarding the phrase "because the eight types of birth do not exist":
this means that [the self] is neither created by itself nor created by another.
If there were a self, it would be created by itself; if there were a Great Brahmā or others, it would be created by another.
Because there would then be that which is produced.
Regarding the phrase "because conditions have no functional activity," it means they do not act simultaneously.
Regarding the phrase "because it is produced by the power of conditions," this means that it is also not produced without a cause.
As the Abhidharma states:
All phenomena do not arise from themselves,
nor do they arise from another,
nor do they arise from both.
It is not that [things] do not arise from two [conditions],
for although there is no active causal condition (*kāraka-pratyaya*), a functional causal condition (*samartha-pratyaya*) can be found.
Nor do they arise from themselves, as this would refute the notion of a self-creator.
"Not born from another" refutes the unequal causes such as Maheśvara;
"not born from both" refutes the Sarvāstivāda position on the nature of causal efficacy;
and "not born without cause" refutes the doctrine of non-causality.
He said: "If the principle of dependent origination dispels both 'self' and 'other,' it is already exceedingly profound."
How much more so when one forgets the four propositions;
therefore, dependent origination is most profoundly deep.
As the *Mūlamadhyamakakārikā* states:
All phenomena do not arise from themselves,
nor do they arise from another; they do not arise from both,
nor are they produced without a cause.
His explanation states:
Because self-nature is empty, there is no arising from self;
because the nature of conditions is empty, there is no arising from another.
Because both self and other are empty, they do not arise together.
If a phenomenon possessed an intrinsic nature, one could speak of it having a cause or being without a cause;
however, since the nature of phenomena is empty, [neither applies].
How can it be said that there is both a cause for existence and no cause?
The first three phrases refute the existence of causal conditions;
the fourth phrase refutes the absence of causal conditions.

is so called because the existence of karma (*karmabhava*) has the capacity to nourish it.
The tenth, the member of existence (*bhavāṅga*), is like medicinal ointment.

the eleven increases have two meanings.

Second, because the subsequent members increase;
for cessation, the reverse of these two applies.

Both the projecting factors and the projected factors are "projecting causes" (*ākṣepahetu*).
Birth, aging, and death are termed "having causes" because the seven factors are their causal phenomena; thus, birth,
aging, and death are termed "suffering that has causes."
Because there is a preceding cause,
craving and grasping— these three being proximate to these two—
are collectively termed suffering.
Because there exists a dharma that is a prior cause.
The Abhidharma states:

At the time of the fruit, there is that which produces and that which is produced;
since maturation and transformation are called "fruit," craving,
grasping, and becoming are also designated by the name "fruit."
Because the fruit arises only when it is about to ripen and transform,

Thirteen [links] are manifested by the exhaustion of the outflows (āsravakṣaya) through three branches.
That is to say, ignorance (*avidyā*), craving (*tṛṣṇā*), and grasping (*upādāna*) are the phenomena of outflow (*āsrava*).
Therefore, the state of their total exhaustion is designated as "that which is manifested by the exhaustion of outflows.
Precisely through the cessation of these three conditions, the remaining links [of dependent origination] are also exhausted.
Therefore, it is said to be manifested by the exhaustion of conditions;
because the contact of afflictions is extinguished, all feelings are extinguished.
Thus, the single member of feeling alone is called "manifested by the exhaustion of feeling."
Regarding the fourteen, seven, and seventy types of knowledge,
Master Jing’s commentary states:
"In order to manifest the knowledge of defiled phenomena that possess causes."
This refers to the statement that dependent origination consists of the factors from aging and death onwards.

Furthermore, it is intended to reveal to those who possess wisdom regarding their own continuum how the defilements they themselves have produced result in aging and death, with birth serving as the condition for their own existence.
This is the statement that there is no aging and death without conditioned arising.
Furthermore, in order to demonstrate that the preceding links have no beginning in time,
it is here stated in general that there is aging and death conditioned by a past birth.
The two phrases "it is not that there is no condition" and "old age and death arise from the past" are stated;
furthermore, the two phrases concerning the future are stated in summary to clarify the various members [of dependent origination] belonging to the posterior limit.

and to reveal that the thorough knowledge (*parijñā*) of the fruits—superior, middling, and inferior—of the three worlds as they abide within their causes is called "knowledge of the abiding of phenomena" (*dharma-sthiti-jñāna*).
This is the explanation of Master Sthiramati.
The response consists of three parts:
first, a general answer regarding the reasons for establishing the wisdoms;
second, a detailed explanation of the reasons for each specific wisdom.
The subsequent summary of the number is a general answer intended to demonstrate to those wise ones that there is a cause for affliction (*saṃkleśa*).
This means observing that each member [of dependent origination] possesses its causal dharma;
that is, for example, old age and death have birth as their cause,
and so on, up to the member of volitional formations having ignorance as their cause.

The wisdom that understands the arising of these defilements is called "wisdom regarding defilement."

and that old age and death do not exist without being conditioned by present birth.
Because one is currently acting as oneself,
the second "and" (ca) further clarifies that there are two types of knowledge regarding past old age and death:
namely, that old age and death exist conditioned by past birth.
It is not that old age and death occur without having past birth as their condition.
When observing the prior limit, one sees that from beginningless time, all instances of old age and death have birth as their condition.

This means that old age and death exist conditioned by future birth;

For although the future has not yet arisen, there is still the possibility of the occurrence of affliction (saṃkleśa) and its cessation (vyavadāna).

Since the first six types of true knowledge (yathābhūta-ñāṇa) are subsumed within the single category of "knowledge of the stability of phenomena" (dhammaṭṭhiti-ñāṇa), they together constitute seven knowledges.
According to this principle,
the noble ones (ārya) also possess the knowledge of the stability of phenomena within their own continuum.
Within the body of an ordinary being (*pṛthagjana*), there is also true wisdom;
all give rise to the contemplation of the seven knowledges.
The same applies to the other ten preceding branches.
Thus, there are seventy-seven [sections].
This master’s division of the text and his explanatory correlations are largely the same as those of Master Bei.
Master Tai further provides an explanation.
The seventh is the thorough knowledge of those phenomena not subsumed under the branches of dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*).

Because one apprehends these phenomena as having substantial existence by means of contaminated knowledge (*sāsrava-jñāna*), it is called "knowledge of the stability of phenomena" (*dharma-sthiti-jñāna*).
Question: It has already been stated that birth is the condition for aging and death, and so forth.
Why, then, is it further stated that "it is not the case that without birth as a condition there is aging, death, and so forth"?
The answer is that there are two types of treatises:
first, those that establish one's own school's tenets (*svasiddhānta*).
Second, the refutation of other schools' positions:
If one were to speak only of birth as the condition for old age and death,
some might harbor doubts, thinking that such a statement made in the context of this discourse does not necessarily accord with the underlying principle.
To resolve that doubt and demonstrate that this principle is certain, it is further stated:
"It is not the case that old age, death, and so forth do not arise conditioned [by other factors].
This constitutes fifteen of the forty-four knowledges.

Question: What is the distinction between the seventy-seven knowledges and the forty-four knowledges?
Answer: In terms of their general characteristics, they arise equally in all three vehicles;
however, in terms of their specific characteristics, both are the contemplations of śrāvakas.
Among the Śrāvakas, those of dull faculties give rise to forty-four knowledges (*jñāna*) to contemplate the fruit by way of the cause,
because this contemplation is easily accomplished.
Those of sharp faculties give rise to seventy-seven knowledges to contemplate how the cause produces the fruit.
Because it is difficult to accomplish through contemplation.
Furthermore, among the seventy-seven knowledges, the second—skill in the aggregates (*skandha-kauśalya*)—is subsumed under the three types of contemplation;
the forty-four knowledges pertain to skill in the four [truths] (*catur-āryasatya-kauśalya*).

Because it serves as the expedient means for the initial arising of the Path, the sixteen [aspects] clarify the arising of supernormal knowledge (abhijñā) and its limitations.
If one is born in the Form or Formless Realms, all [aspects] belonging to the lower stages are excluded from manifesting; they are present only as they are in the Desire Realm.
Master Ji says: This is a door of reasoning that conforms to principle.
In the two upper realms, one does not give rise to any consciousnesses of the lower stages;

Having read extensively, one also masters the flow of literary style and the path of meaning;
as for the gateway to ultimate truth,
within the two upper realms, one excludes those consciousnesses that exist exclusively in the lower stages.
